Result against Martin's markups: every scope item he marked was found blind — 4 storefront openings, 3 aluminum doors, 2 glazing-only lites, hardware sets, sill flashing, 11 detail/section titles, the mirror exclusion — with identical counts and sizes within ½". I missed 4 markups (one detail title, two scope-note blocks, the lite count at the door type) and placed one plan highlight 2' off the wall. I added two implied items he did not mark (jamb break metal, head filler) and marked exclusions he leaves blank.

Convention differences (not scope)

  • Martin highlights the storefront TAG boxes on the plan (A, B, C, D) in the system color; I highlighted the openings only.
  • Martin marks the frame-type LABEL (F1, F4, F5, F6) with a '1 Thus' Qty box beside it; I highlighted the whole frame drawing and the schedule rows, with the Qty box at the schedule row.
  • On elevations Martin places only the Area (W/H/SF); I added a highlight and door circle too.
  • Martin leaves overhead doors, awnings and HM doors blank; I marked them red as considered-and-excluded.
  • Martin highlights detail titles on A-6.1 in Ext SF orange even for the interior S.F. details; I used Int SF (same orange in the toolbox).

What I changed after looking

  • A-1.2 B — My blind box sat 40 pt (≈2'-2") west of the east wall; the grid crop I read stopped at x=2110 so I never saw the wall line. Scope was right, position was wrong.
  • A-3.2 Ext. SF Area — I highlighted the D9 frame but did not carry an Area/SF for the alum door frame F3. Martin did.
  • A-6.2 Ext SF Highlight — Detail title 1/A-6.2 STOREFRONT DOOR THRESHOLD DETAIL — I read it for D2's threshold but didn't mark the title.
  • A-6.1 Ext SF Highlight — Door remark 8: 'storefront doors type A shall be Kawneer medium stile' — a scope note. I used it (medium stile in D2/D3/D9) but didn't mark it.
  • A-6.1 Ext SF Highlight — STOREFRONT NOTES block (tempered at hazardous locations, sill receptors w/ end dams, 1" IG, spandrel black). Used, not marked.
  • A-6.1 Glazing Only Highlight — Door type C vision-lite drawing with '2 Thus' — Martin counts the glazing-only lites at the door TYPE. I counted them on the schedule rows.

Mine only — judgment calls

  • Break metal to match storefront at jamb/sidelite (3/A-6.2) and door jamb (2/A-6.2) — touches our frame, matches our finish. Martin marked only the sill flashing on A-6.1.
  • Double aluminum head filler at the storefront door head (5/A-6.2) — Martin marked the detail title, not the note.

What this test shows

Finding scope was not the hard part on this set. The whole takeoff hung on one sheet, A-6.1, read first: a Storefront Opening Schedule with marks A–D, sizes, frame types and the Kawneer series, plus a door schedule whose material column (AL/GL, HM/GL, HM) sorts every door into ours, glazing-only, or not ours. From there the floor plan carried every mark exactly once, the elevations confirmed sizes to within ½", and the details added the implied items. Reading in your order (schedules → plans → elevations → details) is what made it mechanical.

What was hard, and how it was solved:

  1. Finding the right 19 sheets in 75. The sheet index on the cover named them; a text search for storefront / glass / mirror / skylight across the other 56 confirmed nothing hid in civil, structural or MEP. Cheap and reliable.
  2. Knowing where a thing is, not just that it exists. The vector PDF gives every tag and dimension string as text with coordinates, and every frame line as geometry. Snapping to those lines measured opening A at 10'-8.4" × 10'-0" and the door bay at exactly 3'-0". Your Bluebeam Area on the same frame reads 10'-8⅜" × 9'-1115⁄16. Same answer, no vision model involved.
  3. Rotated sheets. 18 of the 19 architectural sheets are stored rotated 90°. Text and line coordinates come out in the unrotated frame; rendering uses the rotated frame. The current GlazeBid anchoring code does not convert between them, so on this set every snapped box would have landed in the wrong place. This is a one-line fix (multiply by the page's rotation matrix) and it explains part of the July precision numbers.
  4. Conventions vs scope. The 57% box-for-box score against your markups is almost entirely style: you mark the tag box and the frame-type label; I marked the opening and the schedule row. The scorer has to compare scope objects (SF-A found? counted 1? sized right?), not rectangles, or it will punish correct takeoffs.
  5. Trade knowledge did the classifying. Overhead-door lites out, HM lites glazing-only, Bobrick mirror out, break metal that matches storefront in, awning brake metal that matches EIFS out. None of that is visible on the drawing; it came from your rules.

Where it would have been harder: a set with no storefront schedule (McLarty), hand-drawn or scanned sheets, interior-heavy jobs where tags live on enlarged plans, and curtain wall where series alone decides SF vs CW. This set tested the mechanics, not those cases; Curtis and McLarty are next for that reason.

What to build from this (in order): fix rotation handling in the anchoring; make the schedule the first read and the source of the mark list; count marks on plans by tag text, not by vision; snap elevation frames to vector lines for W × H; score by scope object; write markups in your toolbox subjects. Each of those was done by hand here and each is ordinary code.
